title: I/O buffering and fast I/O
relevance: Explains classic cin/getline bugs, flush/TLE pitfalls, and the contest fast-I/O boilerplate interviewers expect.

phases.goal: Establish what stream buffers are, why they exist, and when output is flushed.

must_hit.point: An I/O buffer is an in-memory block owned by the stream (via streambuf) that batches characters so many cheap memory ops replace expensive OS transfers.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions batching/system-call cost and streambuf as the in-memory character store.

must_hit.point: Data path is program ↔ stream buffer ↔ OS kernel buffer ↔ device; cout writes into the stream buffer until flush; cin fills the input buffer in chunks then extractions consume from memory.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Walks the layered path and that input/output hit the kernel only on flush/fill.

must_hit.point: cout is line-buffered on a terminal and fully buffered when redirected; cerr is unbuffered; clog is buffered like cout; cin is fully buffered (often a line at a time from a terminal).
must_hit.evidence_hint: States the per-stream buffering policies, especially cout terminal vs redirect and cerr unbuffered.

must_hit.point: Output flushes when the buffer is full, on newline for line-buffered streams, on explicit flush/endl, on program exit, or when reading from a tied stream (cin tied to cout by default).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists several flush triggers and that cin→cout tie flushes prompts before blocking.

probes: What is a stream buffer, and why don't cin/cout talk to the OS on every character?
When does cout actually flush, and how does cin being tied to cout affect prompts?

hints.1: Think about why a system call per character would be slow.
hints.2: Name the in-memory layer between your program and the kernel, then list flush triggers.
hints.3: Buffer = streambuf batching; flush on full, newline (line-buffered), flush/endl, exit, or tied cin read.

phases.goal: Show how >> and getline consume the input buffer differently, including the leftover-newline trap and stream-state loops.

must_hit.point: operator>> skips leading whitespace, stops at the next whitespace without consuming it, and for string reads one whitespace-delimited word.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States skip-leading, leave-trailing-whitespace, and word-not-line for string.

must_hit.point: After cin >> x, the terminating newline stays in the buffer; the next getline consumes that leftover newline, stores an empty string, and does not wait for the intended line.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains leftover '\n' after >> and empty-string getline as the classic trap.

must_hit.point: Fix by discarding the rest of the line with ignore(max, '\n') or by getline(cin >> ws, s); ignore is preferred when you must clear the current line even if more content followed the token.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives ignore with streamsize max and newline, or ws, and when each fits.

must_hit.point: getline clears then fills the string until delim/EOF/error; consumes but does not store the delimiter; returns the stream so while (getline(...)) works via operator bool as !fail().
must_hit.evidence_hint: Covers delimiter consume-not-store and stream-as-bool loop idiom.

must_hit.point: A failed >> sets failbit and leaves bad characters in the buffer; further I/O is a no-op until clear() then ignore residual input.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says clear then ignore after bad extraction; mentions fail/eof bits for EOF loops.

probes: Why does getline read an empty string right after cin >> n, and how do you fix it?
How do you read until EOF with cin, and what do you do after a failed extraction?

hints.1: Ask what characters >> leaves behind versus what getline treats as end-of-line.
hints.2: Trace buffer after reading a number then Enter; recall stream bool means !fail().
hints.3: >> leaves '\n'; getline takes it as empty line — ignore(max,'\n') or >> ws; EOF loops use while(cin>>x)/getline; recover with clear+ignore.

phases.goal: Contrast flush and sync choices that trade correctness/interactivity for throughput.

must_hit.point: endl writes a newline and flushes every time; in tight loops or large line counts those flushes dominate and can TLE — prefer '\n' and flush once at the end if needed.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts endl (newline+flush) with '\n' and warns about contest TLE from repeated flushes.

must_hit.point: Default sync_with_stdio keeps C++ streams coordinated with C stdio for safe mixing; sync_with_stdio(false) decouples buffers for speed but you must not mix cin/cout with scanf/printf.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains sync purpose, speed win when false, and no-mix caveat.

must_hit.point: cin.tie(nullptr) removes automatic cout flush before each input — faster for bulk I/O, but interactive prompts need an explicit flush yourself.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States default tie vs nullptr and interactivity vs speed.

probes: endl versus '\n' — when does the difference matter?
What do sync_with_stdio(false) and cin.tie(nullptr) buy you, and what do you give up?

hints.1: One choice is about flushing; the other two are contest speed knobs.
hints.2: Separate flush-every-line cost from C-stdio sync and cin↔cout tie.
hints.3: Prefer '\n'; turn off sync and untie for speed; never mix with scanf/printf; flush prompts yourself if untied.

phases.goal: Apply buffer knowledge to contest fast I/O and correct mixed >>/getline or failed-input handling.

must_hit.point: Standard contest boilerplate at start of main before any I/O: ios_base::sync_with_stdio(false); cin.tie(nullptr); then use cin/cout heavily without scanf/printf.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Recites both calls, before-I/O placement, and pick-one-style rule.

must_hit.point: getline still works after sync_with_stdio(false); desync/untie change performance and flush coupling, not the meaning of >> or getline — still need ignore/ws when mixing them.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says getline remains valid; mixing >> and getline still needs the leftover-newline fix.

must_hit.point: Interactive problems may still need ties or explicit flush so the judge sees output before the next read; extreme sizes may use custom readers but the two-liner comes first.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Separates interactive flush needs from bulk contest boilerplate.

probes: How do you speed up C++ I/O in contests, and what caveats apply?
After turning on fast I/O, how do you still correctly read a full line after a formatted >>?

hints.1: Name the two calls people put at the top of main.
hints.2: Explain sync (C++↔C) and tie (flush cout before cin), plus when prompts need flush.
hints.3: sync_with_stdio(false)+tie(nullptr) before I/O; no scanf/printf; '\n' not endl; still ignore/ws before getline after >>.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: endl is newline plus flush; repeated endl in large output loops can dominate runtime and TLE. Prefer '\n' (or "\n") and an optional single flush at the end.
Default sync keeps cin/cout coordinated with scanf/printf so mixing is safe. false decouples buffers for a large speed win but forbids mixing C and C++ I/O on the same streams; call before any I/O.

tradeoffs.topic: cin tied to cout vs cin.tie(nullptr)
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Default tie flushes cout before every cin read so prompts appear; untie removes that cost for bulk contest I/O but you must flush yourself when interactivity requires it.

Use >> for whitespace-separated tokens/numbers (skips leading whitespace, leaves trailing). Use getline when the unit is a whole line including spaces; after >> before getline, discard the leftover newline with ignore or ws.

gotchas.trap: Calling getline immediately after cin >> x and getting an empty string.
gotchas.correction: >> left the terminating newline; getline consumed it as an empty line. Discard with cin.ignore(numeric_limits<streamsize>::max(), '\n') or use getline(cin >> ws, s).

gotchas.trap: Using endl in a tight output loop and getting TLE.
gotchas.correction: endl flushes every iteration. Prefer '\n' and flush once at the end if needed.

gotchas.trap: After sync_with_stdio(false), still mixing cin/cout with scanf/printf.
gotchas.correction: Buffers diverge and I/O can be lost, reordered, or corrupted. Pick one style for the whole program.

gotchas.trap: Calling sync_with_stdio(false) after the first I/O operation.
gotchas.correction: Call it before any I/O; calling after first cin/cout/printf is implementation-defined and may be ignored.

gotchas.trap: cin.tie(nullptr) then printing a prompt without flushing before reading.
gotchas.correction: Untying stops automatic cout flush before cin; flush prompts yourself when the user or judge must see output before the next read.

gotchas.trap: Failed >> leaves the stream unusable and bad characters still buffered.
gotchas.correction: clear() to reset fail/eof bits, then ignore the rest of the line (or residual bad token) before continuing.
